analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a high malware probability (0.9550), and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking (SHAP +0.0068 to +0.0165). However, the evidence is not specific to mining. The highest-ranked n-grams (SUB PUSH, POP SUB, POP LEA, POP PUSH, POP CALL, ADD POP, ADD PUSH, CALL PUSH, OR PUSH, POP RET) are generic stack-frame, prologue/epilogue and call-setup sequences found in almost any compiled x86 program. Their frequencies are very low (0.0004-0.0083), and no function-level locations were provided to tie them to a particular routine. Ranks 11-20 (LEA CALL, CMOVZ MOV, XOR CALL, SUB CALL, CMP CMOVZ, CALL ADD, CALL CALL, MOV JZ, XOR CMOVNZ) have a frequency of 0.000000, so their positive SHAP values come from the model's learned feature distribution, not from observed code in this binary. The CMP/CMOVZ/CMOVNZ and XOR-based pairs hint at branchless or conditional logic, but that is not enough to infer hashing or mining loops. The evidence has no crypto-specific instruction patterns, such as rotate/shift-heavy loops, dense XOR/ADD arithmetic blocks, or SIMD sequences. The classifier's score is therefore consistent with a cryptojacker, but the listed n-grams alone cannot confirm it. The result is inconclusive and needs further verification.

key_indicators: Random Forest malware probability of 0.9550, with all 20 top SHAP contributions positive
Top contributors are generic prologue/epilogue and call-setup n-grams (SUB PUSH, POP SUB, POP PUSH, POP CALL) with low frequencies
Ranks 11-20 have zero observed frequency, so their contribution is model-driven and not backed by observed code
Conditional-move and XOR n-grams (CMOVZ, CMOVNZ, XOR CALL) are weakly suggestive of branchless or bit-manipulation logic but not confirmed
No function-level locations and no crypto-specific instruction patterns (rotates, dense XOR/shift loops, SIMD) in the evidence
analysis.recommended_action: Do not treat this as confirmed cryptojacking from n-gram evidence alone. Run deeper static and dynamic analysis: identify functions containing the observed n-grams, check for hashing or mining loops (heavy arithmetic, rotates, memory-hard routines), inspect imports, strings, and network behavior (pool connections, stratum-like traffic), look for packing or obfuscation, and monitor sustained CPU usage in a sandbox. Escalate to high-confidence only if mining-specific behavior is confirmed.
